definition.text: The chance that the impacts of climate change will cause harm to societies or ecosystems.

facts.text: It covers physical risks, such as extreme weather, and transition risks, the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society.
Risk can also come from the measures people take in response to climate change, not only from the changes themselves.
Climate risk is harder to assess than ordinary hazard risk because the climate no longer stays within a stable range of extremes.
Scientists use climate change scenarios when they analyse climate risk.
Risks are grouped by sector, such as agriculture, water, cities, ecosystems, health and livelihoods.
In 2020 the World Economic Forum ranked climate change as the biggest risk to economy and society.
Adaptation and mitigation can both reduce climate-related risks, and they can work together.

definition.text: The IPCC framework in which climate risk arises from the interaction of three factors: hazards, vulnerability and exposure.

facts.text: Vulnerability measures how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change, formally their propensity to be adversely affected.
Each of the three factors may be uncertain in size and likelihood.
Adaptation can lower climate risk by acting on all three interacting factors.
Global disaster losses have grown mainly because more people and wealth are exposed, though human-caused climate change also plays a part.

definition.text: The ways climate change threatens ecosystems and the services they provide.

facts.text: The main risks are biodiversity loss, changes in ecosystem structure, more tree deaths, more wildfire and losses of ecosystem carbon.
Wildfires and pest outbreaks driven by climate change caused much of the recent tree mortality in North America.
Losing species can raise the risks to ecosystem health.

title: Economic analysis of climate change

definition.text: The use of economic tools and models to estimate how large climate change damages are and who bears them.

facts.text: It studies the costs of climate impacts, the costs and benefits of preventing climate change, and the cost of adapting.
It can also suggest the best mitigation and adaptation policies from an economic point of view.
Its main tools are process-based integrated assessment models, structural models such as CGE and cost-benefit models, and statistical (econometric) methods.
Econometric models estimate how weather and climate affect economic variables, globally or in one sector.
The economics of mitigation is a contentious part of climate policy.
Ordinary economic signals such as the stock market underestimate or cannot value the social benefits of mitigation.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Global economic costs of climate change
article: Economic analysis of climate change#At the global level

definition.text: The total predicted impacts of climate change across all market sectors, plus non-market impacts on ecosystems and health.

facts.text: Estimates rise non-linearly as global average temperature rises.
The 2022 IPCC report found that with about 4 °C of warming and little adaptation, annual global GDP might be 10–23% lower by 2100.
With low warming and more adaptation, the same assessment found GDP reductions of 1–8%.
Total damages are estimated to be 90% less if warming is held to 1.5 °C rather than 3.66 °C.
Losses from extreme weather, climate and water events rose sevenfold from the 1970s to the 2010s.
One study put losses attributable to climate change at an average US$143 billion a year over 2000–2019.
Global estimates handle tipping points poorly and leave out well-being and distributional effects.
Climate impacts add to inflation through higher insurance premiums, energy costs and food prices.

title: Underestimation of climate damages
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Underestimation of economic impacts

definition.text: The argument that economic estimates of climate damages are too low because models leave out tipping points, tail risks and knock-on effects.

facts.text: Tipping points are thresholds beyond which large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the climate system follow.
A 2018 study found global economic impact is underestimated by a factor of two to eight when tipping points are left out.
Many models leave out some climate risks and do not fully trace how damage in one industry or region spreads to others.

contested_note: Economists disagree over whether standard estimates such as the Stern Review's capture the full damages.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Costs of climate change mitigation
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Costs of mitigation

definition.text: The economic cost of actions that cut greenhouse gas emissions or enlarge the carbon sinks that absorb them.

facts.text: Economists estimate the cost of mitigation at between 1% and 2% of GDP.
A 2024 study found keeping warming below 2 °C may cost about 1% of world GDP a year but could prevent losses of 10–20% of GDP by mid-century.
Estimates depend on the baseline scenario, the way costs are modelled and assumptions about future policy.
Early, well-planned action keeps costs down, while delayed global cooperation raises them.
Costs are higher in carbon-intensive, fossil-fuel-exporting and poorer regions when all regions face one carbon value.
Policymakers can compare the marginal abatement costs of different measures, which vary by country, sector and time.
Models assuming perfect markets and policy give low costs; relaxing those assumptions raises estimates, while faster technological learning lowers them.
Economists estimate mitigation costs at between 1% and 2% of GDP, far less than the IMF's estimate of over $5 trillion a year in fossil fuel subsidies.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Sharing the costs of mitigation
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Sharing of mitigation costs

definition.text: The competing proposals for deciding which countries should bear how much of the job of cutting emissions.

facts.text: Equal per capita entitlements, derived from egalitarianism, are the most widely cited way to share abatement costs.
The historical responsibility view bases emission rights on past emissions; two-thirds of today's atmospheric greenhouse gas stock comes from developed countries.
Other proposals rest on basic needs, ability to pay, willingness to pay, or the status quo of current emissions.
Allocating permits by current emissions leaves developing countries worse off, while per capita convergence leaves them better off.

contested_note: No consensus exists on who should bear the costs of mitigation and adaptation.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Costs of climate change adaptation
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Costs of adaptation

definition.text: The costs of planning, preparing for, enabling and carrying out adaptation to climate change.

facts.text: Adaptation benefits can be measured as the damages it avoids.
Every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion.
More resilient infrastructure in developing countries would yield an average of $4 of benefit for each $1 invested.
A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion a year up to 2030.
Another 2023 study, based on national plans from 85 countries, put developing countries' annual adaptation needs at US$387 billion up to 2030.
Both cost and needs estimates are highly uncertain.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Cost–benefit analysis of climate change
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Cost–benefit analysis

definition.text: Applying standard cost-benefit analysis to climate change by turning the good and bad effects of an action into money values.

facts.text: Most climate cost-benefit analyses are done with aggregate integrated assessment models designed for the purpose.
Costs and benefits are valued by willingness to pay or willingness to accept, then discounted to present values.
The usual test for accepting a policy is the Kaldor–Hicks compensation principle: winners could compensate losers and still gain.
Future generations who gain from mitigation cannot compensate the present generation that pays for it.
Valuing impacts on ecosystems and human health is hard, which makes climate cost-benefit analysis controversial.
It may be unsuitable for judging mitigation as a whole, but is still useful for comparing a 1.5 °C target with 2 °C.

contested_note: Sources call the valuation of climate impacts in cost-benefit analysis controversial.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis in climate policy
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Cost-effectiveness analysis

definition.text: A method that ranks policy options by their cost per unit of a set goal, used when benefits are hard to put in money terms.

facts.text: For mitigation the goal is usually tonnes of greenhouse gas cut, giving a cost such as dollars per tonne of CO2.
Adaptation has no common goal, so the measure might be, for example, hectares of land at risk from sea level rise.
It can find the cheapest way to meet a fixed target, such as a sector's emissions cut.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Sequential decision making on climate
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Iterative risk management

definition.text: Handling climate uncertainty by making a series of decisions that are revised as better information arrives.

facts.text: It is closely related to iterative risk management.
Stringent near-term cuts keep open the option of a low stabilization target, such as 450 ppm CO2, which weaker cuts may close.
It weighs the irreversibility of climate damages against the irreversibility of investments to cut emissions.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Equity in climate economics
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Efficiency and equity

definition.text: The debate over who should bear the costs of adaptation and mitigation, on which there is no consensus.

facts.text: One approach charges those who benefit most from the public good of a stable climate.
On a utilitarian basis, an argument can be made for richer countries carrying most of the mitigation burden.
Industrialized countries contributed over two-thirds of the human-made greenhouse gas stock, a stock called an environmental debt.
A 2019 study found climate change had already widened global economic inequality, with poor hot countries growing less.

contested_note: Sources say no consensus exists on who should bear the burden of climate costs, and equity issues cannot be resolved by economics alone.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Ancillary benefits of mitigation
article: Economic analysis of climate change#Ancillary impacts

definition.text: The side effects of mitigation policies, beyond their effect on the climate, which can raise or lower estimated costs.

facts.text: Fewer deaths and less illness are potentially a major side benefit of mitigation.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: Social cost of carbon

definition.text: An estimate, usually in dollars, of the economic damage caused by emitting one more ton of carbon dioxide.

facts.text: By putting climate effects into money terms, it lets policymakers weigh actions that raise or cut greenhouse gas emissions.
It is widely used in regulatory impact analyses, cost-benefit assessments and climate policy.
Its roots lie in Arthur Pigou's 1912 proposal to tax activities that cause negative externalities such as pollution.
Estimates are very sensitive to a few assumptions, above all the discount rate, the damage function and climate sensitivity.
US values have swung from $6 per ton under Trump (7% discount rate) to over $51 per ton under Biden (3% rate).
The SCC is distinct from carbon pricing tools such as taxes or cap-and-trade, though it can inform them.
Some scholars argue its one-extra-ton logic is mismatched to the climate crisis, and that carbon budgets or caps may fit better.

contested_note: Economists, scientists and ethicists criticize the SCC for its sensitivity to assumptions, its ethics and its political volatility.
distinct_from: Calculating the social cost of carbon
Tipping points in the social cost of carbon

title: Calculating the social cost of carbon

definition.text: The chain of steps used to estimate the social cost of carbon, from projecting emissions to discounting future damages.

facts.text: The steps are: project future emissions, model the climate response, assess impacts, put a money value on damages, and discount them.
A low discount rate of 1–2% values future welfare nearly equal to today's; a high rate of 4–5% discounts future damages heavily.
Recent literature supports declining discount rates that start higher and fall over time.
Some versions add a catastrophic risk premium to account for possible disasters and society's dislike of risk.

distinct_from: Tipping points in the social cost of carbon

title: DICE, FUND and PAGE models
article: Social cost of carbon#Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs)

definition.text: The three main integrated assessment models that have historically underpinned social cost of carbon estimates.

facts.text: DICE finds a single global optimal path and assumes damages grow with the square of temperature, without tipping points.
FUND models impacts by region and sector and allows some regions to gain from warming.
PAGE is probabilistic, using Monte Carlo simulations of thousands of futures and modelling catastrophic risks.
Their different methods can give dramatically different values; the Obama-era SCC averaged runs of all three.

distinct_from: Calculating the social cost of carbon
Tipping points in the social cost of carbon

title: Tipping points in the social cost of carbon

definition.text: Extensions to climate-economy models that add abrupt, irreversible damages when warming crosses critical thresholds.

facts.text: Standard models assume smooth, continuous damages, which may underestimate risk.
Modelling studies suggest that including tipping points can double the social cost of carbon.
One method adds a probability of a tipping event times its expected catastrophic damages.

distinct_from: Calculating the social cost of carbon

title: Marginal abatement cost

definition.text: The cost of reducing pollution by one more unit.

facts.text: Marginal cost is the cost of one additional unit, so this measures the cost of the next unit of pollution cut.
It can be negative when the low-carbon option is cheaper than business as usual, but it often rises steeply as more pollution is cut.
A marginal abatement cost curve ranks reductions by their marginal cost.
Policymakers use the curves to see how much abatement is possible at what cost; carbon traders use them to model carbon prices.
Studies worldwide find that making buildings more energy efficient and replacing fossil power with renewables are usually the cheapest cuts.
The curves are criticized for poor transparency and weak treatment of uncertainty, timing, sector interactions and side benefits.

contested_note: The way marginal abatement cost curves are built and used to choose measures has been criticized.

title: DICE model

definition.text: William Nordhaus's integrated assessment model that combines economics, the carbon cycle, climate science and impacts to weigh the costs and benefits of slowing climate change.

facts.text: Nordhaus first proposed it in a 1992 Cowles Foundation discussion paper; a regional variant, RICE, followed in 1996.
It is one of three main models the US Environmental Protection Agency uses to estimate the social cost of carbon.
Its central assumption is that externalities create costs missing from prices, which government must add.
It uses the market return on capital, around 4% on average, as its discount rate.
In 2020, a rerun with updated science and discount rates found the optimal goal was below 2.0 °C of warming, not the 3.5 °C Nordhaus first found.
A 2020 paper with an updated damage function found warming of around 2 °C would be optimal, depending on climate sensitivity.
It treats innovation as external; a variant with induced technical change favours strong early investment in mitigation.
Critics have attacked its sensitivity to assumptions and its choice of discount rate.

contested_note: The model's damage function and discount rate are disputed by critics, and a 2020 rerun changed its optimal warming goal.

title: Integrated assessment modelling

definition.text: A kind of scientific modelling that links the main features of society and the economy with the biosphere and atmosphere in one framework.

facts.text: Its goal is to inform policy-making, usually on climate change.
All climate IAMs include economic processes and the processes that produce greenhouse gases.
They do not predict the future; they estimate what possible scenarios look like.
One split is between process-based models, which map detailed pathways, and aggregate models, which total the costs of climate change and mitigation.
Cost-benefit IAMs such as DICE, PAGE and FUND are the main tools for calculating the social cost of carbon.
Critics say they create an illusory sense of precision and handle justice poorly.
They have been criticized for undervaluing wind and solar power while overvaluing bioenergy and carbon capture.

contested_note: IAMs have been severely criticized for their assumptions, false precision and treatment of uncertainty and justice.

definition.text: Integrated assessment models that map detailed sector-by-sector pathways, used by the IPCC to quantify mitigation scenarios.

facts.text: They have been used to explore pathways for meeting targets such as the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C goal.
They underpin energy policy assessment and simulate the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways.
Well-known frameworks include IMAGE, MESSAGEix, AIM/GCE, GCAM, REMIND-MAgPIE and WITCH-GLOBIOM.
In modelled pathways, BECCS forms a large part of meeting climate targets beyond 2050.

definition.text: A suspected overvaluation of fossil fuel companies, because reserves that cannot be burned within carbon budgets are still counted as valuable.

facts.text: A carbon budget is the upper limit on CO2 emissions that keeps warming below a given level.
In 2011 the Carbon Tracker Initiative found the world could burn only 20% of its fossil fuel reserves to stay below 2 °C.
The rest would become stranded assets, though investors treated them as low-risk.
A 2021 analysis found 90% of coal and 60% of oil and gas reserves could not be extracted for even a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C.
The term was coined by the Carbon Tracker Initiative in reports from 2011 and 2013.
Quarterly results and accounting standards push investors to ignore these long-term risks.
An orderly transition away from fossil fuels could prevent a disruptive bursting of the bubble.

definition.text: The self-reinforcing inertia of large fossil-fuel energy systems that holds back efforts to bring in alternative energy technologies.

facts.text: Gregory Unruh coined the term in a 1999 doctoral thesis.
It arises as technology networks and the institutions and habits that benefit from them grow together, fed by increasing returns to scale.
It explains why cost-effective low-carbon technologies spread slowly, a puzzle called the climate policy paradox.
Car-based transport and fossil-fuel power systems are examples.
A 2007 report sorted lock-in barriers into cost-effectiveness, financial/legal and intellectual property barriers.
Building new natural gas infrastructure risks lock-in and stranded assets.

definition.text: A plausible picture of how the future might unfold, built on a set of assumptions about the main forces driving climate change.

facts.text: Scenarios are used to explore how well mitigation and adaptation will work over the long term.
Pathways are related but more concrete: a roadmap of actions needed to make a scenario come true.
Three key inputs are population, economic activity and new technology.
A baseline scenario is the reference against which an alternative, such as a mitigation scenario, is compared.
Economic growth has been found compatible with both rising and falling emissions, depending on efficiency, energy sources and the shift to services.
Countries use scenarios when drawing up adaptation plans and nationally determined contributions.

definition.text: A possible future in which global warming is reduced by deliberate actions, such as a broad switch away from fossil fuels.

facts.text: A typical one picks a long-range target, such as a CO2 concentration, then fits actions to it, for example a cap on emissions.
They let analysts test the effect of different carbon prices on an economy.
A 550 ppm target, roughly a doubling of pre-industrial CO2, implies about three degrees of warming by conventional estimates.
Reaching a 450 ppm target depends heavily on bioenergy with carbon capture, according to the IEA and OECD.

definition.text: IPCC scenarios that project future greenhouse gas concentrations, not emissions.

facts.text: The original four, RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP6 and RCP8.5, are named for their radiative forcing in 2100 in W/m2.
Higher values mean more emissions, higher temperatures and stronger climate effects.
The IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report began using them in 2014; the Sixth pairs them with the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways.
A study published in 2026 found RCP8.5 no longer plausible.

definition.text: The two main measures of climate sensitivity: the short-term transient climate response and the long-term equilibrium climate sensitivity.

facts.text: The transient climate response is the warming around the time CO2 doubles, in a simulation where CO2 rises 1% a year.
Equilibrium sensitivity is the long-term rise once feedbacks have played out, which can take centuries or millennia.
Equilibrium sensitivity is higher because the oceans buffer warming in the short term.

title: Ethics of climate change

definition.text: The study of the moral questions that climate change raises.

facts.text: Developed countries have gained most from burning fossil fuels, while most climate impacts will fall on the developing world.
Climate change plays out over many generations, setting today's economic and political interests against those of future people.
Economics can predict how policies affect the economy but cannot say which path to choose; that depends on society's values.
Half the world's carbon is emitted by its richest 500 million people, so emissions rise with income wherever one lives.
Poorer people are more exposed to climate effects because they have fewer means to adapt.
Prioritarianism can justify a high discount rate, while utilitarianism favours a low or zero rate.
A rights-based view holds that climate change threatens rights to life, health, food, water, security and shelter.

contested_note: Actors disagree on whether and how far society should act, and on the ethical basis for discounting the future.

definition.text: The duty of people alive now to use resources sustainably and protect the interests of future generations from climate change.

facts.text: Emissions today affect future generations more than the people who cause them.
Pushing impacts onto future people weakens the felt link between cause and effect and can sap the will to act.
Democracies work on election cycles of a few years, while climate change unfolds over hundreds to thousands of years.

definition.text: A probability distribution in which extreme outcomes are much more likely than in a normal or exponential distribution.

facts.text: The most extreme case is a distribution whose tail decays like a power law.
Fitting a normal distribution to fat-tailed data understates the true risk.
Market crashes such as those of 1929, 1987 and 2008 are examples of events that are not mathematically well-behaved.
Martin Weitzman argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails, which standard climate economics handles poorly.

definition.text: Measures of how much of an emitted greenhouse gas stays in the air and for how long, set by the balance between its sources and sinks.

facts.text: The annual airborne fraction of CO2 has been stable at 0.45 for six decades, so 0.55 is taken up by sinks within the first year.
In high-emission scenarios, carbon sinks become less effective, raising the airborne fraction.
A gas's atmospheric lifetime is the time needed to restore equilibrium after a sudden change in its concentration.

definition.text: The division of global greenhouse gas emissions among the sectors of the economy that cause them.

facts.text: About two-thirds of emissions come from burning fuels for energy; the rest come from other processes.
Counted where they are produced, electricity generators make about 25% of global emissions.
Of non-energy emissions, 12% of the total comes from agriculture, 7% from land use change and forestry, 6% from industrial processes and 3% from waste.
Just 5% of the world's power plants produce almost three-quarters of electricity-sector carbon emissions.

title: Cumulative emissions
article: Greenhouse gas emissions#Cumulative and historical emissions

definition.text: Emissions added up over long periods, which indicate who is responsible for the build-up of greenhouse gases in the air.

facts.text: CO2 stays in the atmosphere for at least 150 and up to 1000 years, while methane disappears within about a decade.
Between 1890 and 2007 the US caused 28% of energy-related CO2 emissions, the EU 23% and China 9%.
Over that period developed countries caused 67.8% of total CO2 emissions.
The countries with the highest historical emissions are not always today's largest emitters.

title: Emissions inequality
article: Greenhouse gas emissions#By socio-economic class and age

definition.text: The large gap in greenhouse gas emissions between rich and poor people, driven by a strong link between income and per capita emissions.

facts.text: The richest 1% caused twice as much carbon emissions as the poorest 50% over 1990–2015.
The wealthiest 5% were responsible for 37% of the absolute rise in global emissions.
Annual per capita emissions in industrialized countries are typically up to ten times those in developing countries.

definition.text: An equation that breaks total CO2 emissions into four factors multiplied together: population, GDP per person, energy per unit of GDP, and emissions per unit of energy.

facts.text: It was developed by the Japanese energy economist Yoichi Kaya.
It is a form of the I = PAT equation of Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren for environmental impact.
The factors would cancel out in theory, but it lets emissions be estimated from readily available data.
It shows the levers for cutting emissions, notably energy intensity of GDP and emissions per unit of energy.
It plays a core role in building future emissions scenarios in the IPCC Special Report on Emissions Scenarios.
Energy intensity of GDP has generally declined worldwide, through efficiency, technology and shifts in economic structure.

definition.text: An iterative framework for finding strategies that hold up across many possible futures, exposing their weak points and the trade-offs among them.

facts.text: It is meant for deep uncertainty, where people do not know or agree on how actions lead to outcomes or on the probabilities involved.
It judges policies by robustness rather than optimality, often accepting slightly worse best-case performance for less sensitivity to wrong assumptions.
Instead of predict-then-act, it asks which uncertainties would make a strategy fail, using scenario discovery on large sets of simulations.
It was developed mainly by researchers at the RAND Corporation; an early 1996 study applied it to adaptive strategies for cutting emissions.

definition.text: Scenarios of how global society and economy might change up to 2100, used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report.

facts.text: They pair storylines of alternative socio-economic development with data on population, urbanization and GDP per person.
They are used with integrated assessment models to derive emissions scenarios under different climate policies.
The five are SSP1 Sustainability, SSP2 Middle of the road, SSP3 Regional rivalry, SSP4 Inequality and SSP5 Fossil-fueled development.
IPCC scenario names combine the SSP with forcing in 2100, such as SSP2-4.5.
Projected warming for 2081–2100 ranges from 1.4 °C under SSP1-1.9 to 4.4 °C under SSP5-8.5.
A 2025 assessment put median warming under current policies at about 2.7 °C by 2100, closest to SSP2-4.5.

title: Stern Review

definition.text: A 700-page review of the economics of climate change released for the UK government in October 2006 by economist Nicholas Stern.

facts.text: It called climate change the greatest and widest-ranging market failure ever seen.
Its main conclusion is that the benefits of strong, early action far outweigh the costs of not acting.
Without action, it estimated losses equal to at least 5% of global GDP each year, possibly 20% or more counting wider risks.
It proposed investing 1% of global GDP a year; in 2008 Stern raised this to 2% because climate change was faster than expected.
Its near-zero pure rate of time preference, which Stern held to be the only ethical choice, was the most debated point.
Economists were split: some called it deeply flawed while others, including Kenneth Arrow, judged its main conclusion justified.
In 2008 Stern said the Review had underestimated the risks and damages of warming.

contested_note: Economists disagree sharply over the Review's discount rate, damage estimates and mitigation costs.

title: Green paradox

definition.text: Hans-Werner Sinn's argument that climate policy expected to tighten over time pushes fossil fuel owners to extract faster, speeding up global warming.

facts.text: Policies that will get greener lower future fuel prices more than current ones, so owners extract more now and invest the proceeds in capital markets.
Countries that do not cut demand burn both the carbon freed by green countries (leakage) and the extra carbon extracted early.
Sinn argues climate policy must target the supply side, for example by taxing resource owners' capital gains or a global emissions trading cap.
Critics note that Sinn overlooks large government support to fossil fuels, put at US$160–200 billion a year in OECD and key emerging economies.

contested_note: The source calls the book controversial, and its claims about renewable support are disputed.

definition.text: A set of methods for measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organization emits.

facts.text: Organizations use it to set an emissions baseline, set reduction targets and track progress.
It works at scales from companies and cities to national greenhouse gas inventories.
Carbon credit markets depend on accurate measurement of emissions and reductions.
Standards such as the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and ISO 14064 group emissions into Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased energy) and Scope 3 (value chain).
Scope 3 is often the largest source of corporate emissions and the hardest to report accurately.
There is some evidence that programs requiring GHG accounting help to lower emissions.
It helps investors understand the climate risks of companies they invest in.

title: PAGE model

definition.text: A probabilistic integrated assessment model, one of the three main models behind estimates of the social cost of carbon.

facts.text: It uses Monte Carlo simulations to model thousands of possible futures, with a probabilistic treatment of catastrophes and tipping points.
It tends to give higher social cost of carbon estimates with wide uncertainty bands.
Chris Hope of Cambridge University designed the PAGE2002 version used in the Stern Review.

notes: Phrase concept; also covered jointly by the 'DICE, FUND and PAGE models' entry (part02).

title: FUND model

definition.text: An integrated assessment model that estimates climate damages region by region and sector by sector, used for the social cost of carbon.

facts.text: It models impacts such as agriculture, health and sea level rise by region and includes some adaptation over time.
It allows negative damages, meaning some regions or sectors gain from warming.
Its assumptions about adaptation and warming benefits can understate damages.
It is Richard Tol's model; a reviewer of the Copenhagen Consensus said relying on it alone was not reasonable.

notes: Phrase concept; also covered jointly by the 'DICE, FUND and PAGE models' entry (part02).

definition.text: Uncertainty so great that decision-makers do not know or agree on how actions lead to outcomes or on the probabilities of key inputs.

facts.text: Robust decision-making describes it with ranges or sets of plausible probability distributions rather than one best estimate.
Decision-making under deep uncertainty may use many climate scenarios to test actions across different possible futures.
The DICE model has been criticized for ignoring deep uncertainty, which tends to lower its social cost of carbon.
